newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO struggles for deals on infotech, labour rights.
newsitem.headline: WTO struggles for deals on infotech, labour rights.

text.p: Trade ministers scrambled on Wednesday to reach an accord aimed at cutting tariffs on information technology while struggling to reconcile deep-seated differences over workers' rights.

Negotiators from the United States and the European Union scheduled another round of meetings on the sidelines of a 128-nation trade conference in Singapore to settle their remaining disagreements over the outline of an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) after meeting in four closed-door sessions on Tuesday.
"There is not an agreement yet," European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said on Wednesday after meeting Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.
"There is agreement on many points. There are some outstanding ones. We are trying to resolve those," Brittan said.

The United States, with strong backing from Japan, is keen to see an accord to free up trade in the $600 billion market for computers, software chips and other high-technology products by the year 2000 before the end of this week's first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

"There is no question that what the industrialised countries now hope for most here is a deal on information technology products and agreement to work hard for a basic telecommunications pact by February," said one key negotiator.

The Big Four trade powers -- the United States, the EU, Japan and Canada -- hope to settle their differences, in particular over the touchy question of product coverage, before meeting again later on Wednesday with other nations interested in joining the infotech accord.

"They (the Big Four) are still fighting. Some working-level negotiators of some countries are getting crazy," a Japanese givernment source told Reuters. "I am hopeful we will reach a consensus before the afternoon meeting starts."

Developing countries were shown a draft outline late on Tuesday of an accord worked out by the Big Four, but the draft did not specify product coverage or spell out what sort of flexibility could be shown to developing countries on the timing of the tariff cuts, the Japanese source said.

Progress on the infotech deal looked less elusive than on the contentious issue of whether the 128-nation WTO, set up in 1995 as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, should get involved in enforcing labour standards.

The United States, with strong backing from France and Norway, says that without action to tackle the exploitation of child labour and eradicate sweatshop conditions in the Third World, support for free trade in rich countries will evaporate.

Diplomats said that Washington, digging in its heels, had repeated a threat to reject other parts of the meeting's final declaration to be published on Friday unless it won mention of the labour issue.

Poorer countries are equally adamant in rejecting a scrutiny role for the WTO. They say attempts to impose workplace rules is protectionism in disguise because the trade advantages their cheap labour gives them would be whittled away.
On Wednesday, Malaysia again rejected the attempts to put labour rights on the official WTO agenda.
"The debate on the issue of labour standards has indeed proven to be a divisive factor, Rafidah Aziz, Malaysia's international trade and industry minister, said in a speech.
"We reject any move to discuss and deliberate labour standards and other social clauses in the WTO," Rafidah said.

Bill Jordon, secretary-general of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), told a news conference he was hopeful some compromise could be reached, but said it might take the form of a statement asking the WTO director-general to take up the issue with his counterpart at the International Labour Organisation (ILO).

"I am hopeful that the two extremes of this argument can find a place within one statement," Jordan said. "I did not expect the WTO to take on board all that we want...what we want them to do is to recognise their responsibility in the process of the globalisation of trade."

Delegates have meanwhile been edging towards consensus on textiles and agriculture, as well as over how the world trade body should tackle government procurement, investment rules and domestic competition policy.
